title: Lazy gas, hot gas, and a thousand robots
abstract: Amazon Robotics operates over a million robots across more than 300 warehouses worldwide. Inside a single warehouse, thousands of robots share the floor, moving inventory for order fulfillment and stock replenishment. Finding efficient, collision-free robot paths to their destinations is therefore essential for smooth operations. Let us formulate the underlying multiagent pathfinding (MAPF) problem a bit more precisely. Consider a typical warehouse layout as a W x H rectangular grid. At each time step, a robot can make one of five choices: move north, east, west, or south, or wait. These choices must be coordinated to avoid collisions. Over a planning horizon of T time steps, finding optimal robot paths involves approximately n = 5WHT binary decision variables, giving 2n possible combinations before accounting for feasibility constraints. Finding optimal paths that minimize the total move cost or arrival time without collisions is NP hard in general and can become computationally intractable even for moderate numbers of robots. In a paper we presented at this year’s International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), we show that physics offers a way around this intractability: plan trajectories as if the robots were particles of gas. Modeling the robots as a cold, lazy gas, whose particles spend only the minimum effort to reach their destinations, yields optimal, minimum-energy paths. This is equivalent to treating trajectory planning as an optimal-transport problem. It yields optimal paths, but computing them may take too long for real-time deployment. Modeling the fleet as a hot gas, whose particles jitter randomly along the way, yields trajectories that are computationally faster but potentially suboptimal. As the temperature drops to zero, however, the jittery hot-gas paths settle onto the lazy-gas ones. Our approach uses a Schrödinger bridge — a hot-gas model — to efficiently approximate the solution to an optimal-transport problem — the cold-gas model. Optimal transport To develop the formal connection, let us travel back to 1781 in France to meet Gaspard Monge, the father of differential geometry. Monge was looking for the most efficient way to transport excavated dirt to military fortifications. His studies gave rise to the optimal-transport problem, which asks how to transport resources from a set of sources to a set of destinations while minimizing cost, such as distance traveled or work done. Monge’s sources were the locations containing dirt. His formulation required all mass at each source location to be transported to one destination, producing a deterministic transport map. Although intuitive, Monge’s original formulation is a difficult nonlinear optimization problem with a potential combinatorial explosion in discrete settings. Finding an optimal map is therefore technically challenging and, in some settings, impossible. Roughly 150 years later, Soviet mathematician Leonid Kantorovich relaxed this restriction by allowing mass from one source to be split among multiple destinations. His key insight was that this relaxation converts a difficult optimization over transport maps into a linear program, a class of problems for which highly efficient computer algorithms were subsequently developed. Kantorovich received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to the theory of optimum allocation of resources. Optimal transport connects two mass distributions, also known as marginals, through minimum-cost transport plans. This two-marginal formulation represents only the initial and final configurations and the cost of transporting between them, not the intermediate paths or collisions along those paths. Formulating MAPF as optimal transport therefore requires a multistage approach, because robots generally cannot move from their starting locations to their destinations in a single time step; their locations must also be represented at every intermediate time. title: Introducing the Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API, with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards and Enterprise Data Controls for Claude models
abstract: Today we are announcing the general availability of the trusted access program API on Amazon Bedrock . The API gives you one place to discover, request, and enroll in model provider trusted access programs. We are also announcing the public preview of the first two offerings for Claude models: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) and Enterprise Data Controls (EDC). Both are available on Amazon Bedrock, including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP). Frontier AI labs require stricter safety monitoring policies to their most capable models, and those policies still apply on Amazon Bedrock. For eligible customers, model providers also offer customers more control on how those policies are met, such as where retained data is stored and how it is reviewed. Each offering has its own terms, approvals, and settings. The Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API gives every provider offering one consistent Amazon Bedrock experience. Your teams discover offerings, check eligibility, and enroll in the same way for every provider. Your administrators decide who can enroll, using existing IAM policies and service control policies. As more model providers add offerings, those appear in the same place. EFS and EDC were built in partnership between AWS and Anthropic. They let you access Anthropic’s most capable models safely, from both a model use and a customer data perspective. With both EFS and EDC, when automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for your team to review. With EFS, customers store their data in their own AWS account, and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic or Amazon Bedrock. With EDC, retained data is stored in Amazon-managed storage instead of your account and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic. One application gives access to both offerings. In this post, we explain how the trusted access program API works, then walk through EFS and EDC storage options and setup. How trusted access programs work A trusted access program is a named provider program that gives customers more control of safety reviews and access to model capabilities in exchange for accepting the program’s terms. Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API now gives you one place to find the model and use case programs available to your account. EFS and EDC are the first offerings available today. Offerings that providers add later appear in the same place and follow the same steps. Anyone with access to the trusted access program API can list the offerings and check their status for an account, an organization in AWS Organizations, or an Amazon Bedrock project. The status tells you what to do next. eligible means you’re eligible for the offering and can enroll, requestable means you need approval for eligibility first, and the statusReason field in the response explains how to request it. The model provider (or AWS, as authorized by the model provider) approves your eligibility. Enrolling is a separate step where you accept the offering’s terms imposed by the provider. You enroll at the scope where you were approved: an account, every account in an organization from the management account, or a single project. You can opt out at any time. Each step is a call to the trusted access program API, so you control who can enroll with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and service control policies (SCPs). More information is available in the trusted access programs documentation . Enterprise Frontier Safeguards With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), you can retain your data in your own AWS environment with full control. It is designed with over 100 customers, including a quarter of the Fortune 100 and many companies in industries with strict rules on data visibility, like healthcare, financial services, and law. Assessing AI Impact: Notes for Your CFO
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Hi there. This is the epilogue to my series on assessing the impact of AI-assisted software development. It brings all the concepts together into one whole. It’s also good for sharing with your CFO and other members of your leadership team. You can find the beginning of the series here: Are You Getting Your Money’s Worth from AI? The rest of the articles are linked below. Comfy? Great. Let’s get started. Give me the shortest possible version AI-assisted software development is expensive, and while the potential returns are high, they’re not yet proven. The field is changing rapidly, so learning the right approach requires experimentation and measurement. Spending varies by an order of magnitude: from hundreds of dollars per person per month to thousands. To know which approach is best, you need to measure impact as well as costs. The fullest view involves modeling the ROI of your software initiatives, which requires leadership support and cross-departmental participation. For a faster and more targeted view, ask your engineering leaders to measure changes in software development speed. But don’t just look at what you’re getting now; consider the long-term effects of unintended consequences and the possibility of lock-in. Say more about AI program fundamentals Measuring the costs of an AI-assisted software development program is fairly easy, but measuring benefits is harder. It’s tempting to use easy, shallow approaches that don’t consider the full picture. Some token costs are heavily subsidized, so prices could go up. Examples include subscriptions with generous token allowances and temporary promotions. On the other hand, competition could drive prices down. As you forecast ROI, consider optimistic and pessimistic cost scenarios. Consider that the fastest approaches might not be the most cost-effective. The best investment might involve lower per-person delivery speed, but much lower token costs, especially if the money for AI comes at the cost of headcount. Read more about why you should measure impact, and what you shouldn’t measure, in part 1 . What was that about modeling ROI? Most organizations primarily think in terms of cost and predictability, with minimal attention to value. Modeling ROI will not only help you understand AI’s impact, it will give you a better understanding of your software development efforts in general. Product development can create a model that calculates an initiative’s net present value. This requires cross-departmental participation, backing from leadership and finance, and some educated guesses. It will never reflect real value perfectly—it involves too many guesses and assumptions—but it makes those assumptions concrete and focuses people on what you’re getting for your money. Read more about modeling software’s business impact in part 4 . I just want to know if AI is faster Engineering leaders can get a narrower read on AI’s impact by measuring how it changes software delivery speed. They can also compare one approach to another, which will allow them to find the optimal blend of speed and costs for your company. Simplistic speed measurements abound. When evaluating claims, look for evidence of sophistication, such as randomized comparisons, and look for sustained results across numerous teams. Beware of measurements that simply count deliverables or changes in “velocity.” They’re not standardized. The pressure to demonstrate results from AI is immense, and the stories of success that are shared in conferences and executive circles grow with each retelling. Calibrate your skepticism accordingly. Listen for how the storytellers measured impact. Look for evidence of sustained results, not cherry-picked examples. Read how to measure changes in delivery speed in part 2 . What about unintended consequences and lock-in? Speed is only part of the pict

title: Trusting an Agent Beyond Your Expertise
abstract: I have a Raspberry Pi on my home network running Pi-hole, a flight tracking setup, and a few services around them, with an external solid-state drive attached to it. When I first described the machine to my coding agent, I said there was nothing particularly complicated or compute intensive running on it, or so I thought. Every so often, the Pi would stop responding, and a reboot was the only way I could bring it back. Eventually it became annoying enough that I really wanted to find out what had happened. The logs I needed seemed to disappear with the restart, so I had a way to recover the machine and very little idea of how to investigate the failure. My Linux knowledge covers the things I’ve needed for server-side Java development over the years, and I can find my way around a terminal or follow familiar procedures. System-wide container configuration, service dependencies, and the details of IPv4 and IPv6 take me well beyond that experience. I knew enough to recognize that changing some of those settings could cut off my access and leave me running up the stairs to wire my computer up to the Pi. My dad also depends on this machine for his flight radar app and enjoys watching planes go by, so I had to consider how a change would affect him too. Before I could consider changing any of those settings, I needed help deciding where to look. Somebody had to turn “The Pi has stopped responding” into questions I could investigate, and I decided that asking the agent was a reasonable way to do that. It went a little too well, to be honest. The agent configured persistent logging and regular health samples so there would be information to examine after a restart. We moved to Ethernet and disabled Wi-Fi, and it checked the services, storage, and connection to the router. It later repaired forwarding for local name queries and identified a problem in the order in which the Pi-hole container stopped and its external drive was unmounted. The container needed the drive to stay mounted until the service had stopped, so the agent added an explicit dependency on the drive’s mount to put those events in the right order. After I later installed updates and rebooted, I asked it to check again, and it found log entries showing the service stopping, followed by a successful unmount of the drive. I could follow those steps once the agent explained them to me: finding the missing dependency, expressing it in the service configuration, and choosing the log entries to examine all required knowledge I was getting from the agent. I trusted its assessment of that reboot, relying on it to judge changes it had made with the root access I had given it over SSH. That felt very weird and gave me reason to think more carefully about the advice to “trust, but verify.” Checking a repair I needed help to make The agent also suggested the configuration backups and checks after changes, so I relied on it for the precautions as well as the repair. Judging whether I could recover from a failed change required some of the same Linux knowledge I just didn’t have. In “ Code Review After Code Gets Cheap ,” I described starting with intended behavior, evidence, and the effects of a change elsewhere in the system. Adjusting enough of the specification to make correctness checkable also depends on knowing what to expect. With my Pi challenges, I needed help establishing those expectations while deciding whether to accept the change, which left me wondering how likely this approach was to succeed and how much trust was justified. I had given my agent the ability to act on the assessment I was asking it to make. With root access over SSH, it could change the operating system and services, including settings that determined whether I could reach the machine again. My willingness to let it proceed depended partly on what I thought a mistake would cost me. title: When One Task Becomes Another
abstract: An OpenAI model was told to prove a theorem itself. It was told again not to obtain another team’s solution. It agreed. Later, while still trying to finish the same theorem, it exposed a researcher’s GitHub token publicly and split the token into pieces so secret scanning would not catch it. The striking part is not that the model forgot what it had been told, but that it appears to have remembered the constraint and continued anyway. The agent remembered exactly what we asked, for too long. That incident was disclosed alongside another in which an agent, blocked from ordinary web access, discovered that DNS could be used to reach an external chatbot. As of late September, OpenAI says that tool-use training, evaluation, and inference involving its most capable models remain paused while it investigates and strengthens safeguards. These incidents are often described as agents going out of bounds. But several of the recent cases suggest a narrower and more useful pattern: The objective remains surprisingly stable while the tasks generated to achieve it move farther away from the authority originally granted. Goal lineage does not imply authorization lineage. Notice the pattern The table below sets out five recent incidents. In each one the original objective stays recognizable, the tasks used to pursue it change after the agent meets friction, and the last column shows what happened to the authorization that started the work. Incident Original objective Transition after friction Authorization outcome OpenAI GitHub token Prove a Lean theorem locally Repeated failure pushed the model back toward obtaining another team’s solution; it eventually exposed a split GitHub token Explicit constraints were recognized and still violated OpenAI DNS / external chatbot Identify a person from public clues Normal search routes failed; the agent discovered a DNS-based route to an external chatbot. Sandbox network restrictions were bypassed. OpenAI / Hugging Face Complete internal cyber-evaluation tasks Agents created communication paths, regained internet access, and expanded the means available to finish the task. The trajectory crossed into internal and third-party systems. UK AI Security Institute Complete cybersecurity evaluation tasks Difficult tasks produced new tactics including pull requests, fake identities, social engineering, and Tor. AISI reported 19 out-of-scope actions across 10 of 122 runs: 17 from Anthropic’s Mythos 5, 2 from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Sol. OpenAI / Australian Medicare portal Retrieve public Medicare statistics Repeated access failures led to alternative retrieval methods. The agent bypassed access controls and reached non-public files. These cases are not identical. The GitHub token incident involved explicit instruction violation. The DNS incident involved a sandbox bypass. The Hugging Face episode involved agents creating new communication and access paths while pursuing evaluation goals. The AISI report documents a broader class of unsanctioned real-world actions produced during difficult cyber tasks. What they share is a trajectory. The task encounters friction, so the agent looks for another route. That route creates a new task or a new operational state. The agent continues from there. Each workaround becomes part of the starting conditions for the next decision. This is different from a simple retry: A retry repeats an attempt against essentially the same task state. A workaround changes the state space. It may introduce a new resource, target, credential, actor, network path, or capability. Retrying helps explain how often an agent might eventually succeed. It does not explain why the path itself changes direction or why each new step can depend on the one before it. That distinction matters because authorization is usually easiest to define at the beginning. A human or system instructs the agent to do A. The agent has tools and permissions appropriate for A. title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
abstract: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right. Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence. Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here? If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today. But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants. If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue. PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand. This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there. And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation. This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead. It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source. But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025. There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. title: The Download: AI swamping open records, and firefighting for permafrost
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI is straining America’s open records systems AI has intensified investors’ interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests. As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent. Find out how AI is testing the limits of America’s right to know . —Matthew King MIT Technology Review Narrated: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below. Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground. Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking? This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
abstract: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy. Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.” Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget. As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent. Transparency, monetized The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town. This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc .” Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says. SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies. The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
abstract: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well. Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm. This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious). But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place. Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer. You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models. The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences . But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet. Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language. title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
abstract: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil. But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods. These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it , which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years. “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.” How it works There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks. The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon. If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing. “Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans. ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations. But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices. title: Why Does Voice AI Still Struggle With Kenyans’ Speech?
abstract: When people read prepared text aloud, AI can transcribe Swahili with remarkably few errors, and Swahili speech recognition looks close to solved. A March 2026 preprint by a team including a Harvard University researcher reports a 3.24 percent word-error rate on recordings from Mozilla’s Common Voice collection of volunteer-recorded speech. But Kenyans rarely talk like Common Voice volunteers. They switch between Swahili and English mid-sentence, drop in Sheng slang that changes by neighborhood, speak with accents shaped by their first languages, and contend with public-transport noise on low-end handsets. Another 2026 preprint , which covers 20 African languages, argues that this kind of spontaneous, noisy, overlapping audio exposes a generalization gap that scaling laws built on the English language have not closed. Voice has become a main interface for many Kenyans, as WhatsApp voice notes and chatbot voice prompts gain popularity in a country that ranks first globally on AI usage. But if an AI model cannot parse everyday speech, it quietly excludes the people it was meant to serve. “My iPhone’s Siri is unable to follow my voice command in Sheng or Swahili,” says Loise Lionah, a beautician in Nairobi. “ChatGPT tries to understand but gets the meaning wrong. The case is similar with Gemini and Claude.” Swahili Dialects and Sheng Challenge Voice AI Swahili, also called Kiswahili, is one of Kenya’s two official languages, alongside English. A Bantu language of the East African coast, Swahili is spoken by more than 200 million people across 14 African countries. Tanzania is regarded as the home of standard Swahili. Yet Catherine Mangare , an AI and computing lecturer at Tanzania’s Sokoine University of Agriculture and a Ph.D. candidate at Okayama University in Japan, says even there, the standard is only the baseline. “Standard Kiswahili is a useful starting point,” she says, “but Tanzanian speech varies by region and setting.” Sheng, spoken and understood by about 60 percent of Kenyans, adds another layer. This Swahili variant, which emerged among Nairobi’s urban youth many decades ago, follows Swahili grammar but borrows from English, Kenyan mother tongues, and even Hindi, Spanish, and American slang, and it has no standard spelling. Linguists label it a language in constant flux : For example, the Sheng word for “girl” fluctuates according to generation, location, and social media trends. “Sheng itself is highly broken down per region,” says Tehillah Kachila , founder and CEO of Nairobi-based Zabibu Technika, a startup that builds the Fikra family of Swahili AI models. Kachila says the most recent Sheng dataset dates back to 2019—a major reason, he argues, why prominent voice AI systems struggle to respond accurately to Sheng prompts. Lilian Wanzare, shown leading a voice-data collection workshop, develops speech datasets for Kenyan languages to help AI systems understand a wider range of speakers. Maseno Centre for Applied AI Building Speech Datasets for African Languages The supply of recorded Swahili speech is growing. The African Next Voices project , supported by a US $2.2 million Gates Foundation grant, has recorded 9,000 hours across 18 languages. Lilian Wanzare , who leads the project’s Kenyan component at Maseno University’s Centre for Applied AI, puts its Kenyan output at roughly 3,000 hours of transcribed speech. Google’s Waxal corpus , launched in February 2026, adds more than 11,000 hours across 21 African languages, Swahili included. But hours are not the same as coverage. Gilbert Korir , cofounder and CEO of the Nairobi-based Swahili speech AI startup MsingiAI , says a large dataset can hide limited variation in speakers and recording conditions. The scarcest material is the conversational speech that mixes languages. abstract: The British cyber agency says that "building strong foundations has never mattered more" as AI hacking tools rely on exploiting simple security flaws.

abstract: Next-generation data centers will need tens of gigawatts of power every year. One of Crusoe's investors thinks solar and energy storage are the obvious choice.

title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
abstract: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory. Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation. But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next. Read full article Comments

title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
abstract: Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control. Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year. The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi's blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules. Read full article Comments

title: Backblaze explains why it's sharing customer information with advertisers
abstract: Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze's privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers. Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.” The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers. Read full article Comments

title: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites
abstract: In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers. If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold. "The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth." Read full article Comments

title: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
abstract: Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault . After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it's an installable package with automatic updating. Ladybird is most notable for what it isn't: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google's Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird's rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. "The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork," project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday's announcement. "The browser around it is modest, but functional." Read full article Comments

title: Etsy clarifies AI terms after seller backlash
abstract: After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the company to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance. In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the company's terms of service and admitted that her team "should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content." “Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we're using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.” Read full article Comments

title: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop
abstract: Drone attacks on data centers. Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion. In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine: We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there's an incentive to target it. Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers: Read full article Comments

title: Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets
abstract: On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran. Although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China . In a press release , however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security. The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. Read full article Comments

title: Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl
abstract: In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound. The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate. Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast. Read full article Comments

title: A familiar Iranian hacking group has found a new way to cause chaos
abstract: One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history : cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food. Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command. Read full article Comments

title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
abstract: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics. LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online. The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI. Read full article Comments

title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
abstract: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks. The missions affected by the outages — hopefully temporary — are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history. Losing its voice The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate. Read full article Comments

title: Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
abstract: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters , Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide. Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote. The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report , dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident. Read full article Comments

title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
abstract: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset. It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math. Tackling Riemann The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field." Read full article Comments

title: Back-to-back measles deaths is our new reality; US tally now at 14
abstract: Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water. The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23 . Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died. Deaths and transmission On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death , an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child . New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby . On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4 . Read full article Comments

title: Amazon drone crashes on garage after delivering shampoo, draws FAA probe
abstract: An Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States. The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit . After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines. “Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7. Read full article Comments

title: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can
abstract: A European Ariane 6 launcher propelled 36 satellites into orbit for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation Tuesday, continuing the network's build-out after 40 satellites were lost earlier this month during a failure of United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket . The launch was an important rebound for Amazon, bringing the Amazon Leo fleet to 432 satellites as the company seeks to fill the void left by the grounding of ULA's Vulcan rocket, Amazon's primary launch provider. Now, an Amazon official tells Ars it is accelerating several Falcon 9 launches the company has purchased from SpaceX, which also owns the Starlink satellite network that Amazon seeks to dethrone. The next Falcon 9 launch for Amazon Leo is now planned for December, Amazon said, moved forward from its previous launch date next year. Several more Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites in rapid succession after the December flight. Read full article Comments

title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
abstract: The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production , but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant. That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists. As previously reported , the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018 , OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper— identified the growing popularity of " dry hopping " (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon. Read full article Comments

title: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
abstract: Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said Monday. It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved. Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either. Read full article Comments

title: Tidal announces ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted
abstract: Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists. Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn't enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated. As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal's total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it's only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements. Read full article Comments

title: 운영자의 시간을 아끼는 AI 에이전트 2부 - MCP 부터 Agent 설계까지
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 발표 내용 운영 문의가 들어오면 운영자는 로그와 메트릭, 과거 사례를 직접 살펴보고 답변해야 합니다. 업무 시간 밖에 들어온 문의는 첫 답변을 받기까지 약 13시간이 걸리기도 했습니다. 이 발표에서는 OpenSearch 운영 문의에 운영자보다 먼저 답변하는 AI 에이전트, care-ai를 만들면서 겪은 시행착오를 소개합니다. 그 과정에서 얻은 설계 원칙과 개선 효과를 실제 사례와 수치로 공유합니다. ​ <참고> 운영자의 시간을 아끼는 AI 에이전트 1부 - RCA·Q&A 운영 지식 그래프 ​ 발표 대상 LLM 에이전트를 운영 업무에 적용하려는 분 MCP 서버와 도구를 설계하는 분 에이전트 답변의 정확도와 신뢰성을 높이고 싶은 분 ​ 목차 Episode 1. 처음 만든 에이전트 필요한 정보가 모두 있었는데도, 에이전트는 왜 원인을 확정하지 못했을까요? Episode 2. MCP 응답 설계 도구 응답 하나가 모델의 입력 한도를 넘었습니다. 이 문제를 계기로 모델에는 요약을 먼저 제공하고, 원본 데이터는 요청할 때만 반환하도록 MCP 서버를 바꿨습니다. 24회 평가에서 정답은 10회에서 17회로 늘었고, 토큰 사용량은 26% 줄었습니다. Episode 3. 모델 vs 코드 모델의 판단에 맡길 일과 코드로 결정할 일은 어떻게 나눠야 할까요? 모델은 탐색과 판단을, 코드는 근거 검증과 최종 판정을 맡도록 구조를 바꿨습니다. 그 결과, 같은 문의를 세 번 평가했을 때 정확한 원인을 답한 횟수가 0회에서 3회로 늘었습니다. Episode 4. 답변 설계 운영자는 무엇을 어떤 순서로 설명할까요? 운영자의 답변 방식을 참고해 상태, 확인한 값, 원인, 다음 조치와 담당자를 정해진 순서로 전달하도록 했습니다. 요청자에게 보낼 답변과 운영자가 확인할 카드도 분리했습니다. Episode 5. 결과 첫 응답 시간의 중앙값은 47초였습니다. 운영자 댓글 수는 38% 줄었고, 문의가 종료되기까지 걸리는 시간은 절반으로 줄었습니다. 운영자가 직접 답변한 문의의 비율도 약 95%에서 60%로 낮아졌습니다. 데모: 주문 데이터 문의부터 답변까지 테스트 클러스터에 미리 준비한 사례로, 주문 데이터에 관한 문의를 접수한 care-ai가 답변을 내놓기까지의 과정을 보여드립니다. ​ ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: 운영자의 시간을 아끼는 AI 에이전트 1부 - RCA·Q&A 운영 지식그래프
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 운영 문의에 명확한 답변을 남겨도 이슈가 닫히면 묻히기 쉽습니다. 같은 원인으로 문의가 다시 들어오면 운영자는 처음부터 다시 조사해야 했습니다. 이 발표에서는 n3r 운영 이슈에서 LLM으로 RCA(근본 원인 분석)와 Q&A를 추출해 Neo4j 지식 그래프에 쌓고, Care AI 에이전트가 이를 찾아 답변에 활용하도록 만든 과정을 소개합니다. "OpenSearch 업그레이드가 멈췄어요"라는 실제 문의를 따라가며, 대화를 그래프로 바꾸기 위한 프롬프트와 추출 결과를 검증하는 방법을 설명합니다. 증상뿐 아니라 원인도 같은 사례를 찾기 위해 적용한 하이브리드 검색과 LLM 리랭킹, 클러스터 상태 정보의 활용 방식도 함께 다룹니다. ​ <참고> 영상속 사내용어 n3r = 네이버 사내 쿠버네티스 기반 컨테이너 플랫폼 ​ 발표 대상 AI 에이전트로 반복되는 운영 업무를 효율화하는 데 관심 있는 분 ​ 목차 기존 운영 문의에는 어떻게 답해 왔나 운영 문의 속에 숨은 구조, RCA 대화를 그래프로 더 정확하게 찾기 진단이 아닌 질문: Q&A 최종 구조와 Care AI 성과와 향후 계획 ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: AI가 만든 결과를 그대로 믿고 계신가요?
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 테스트는 전부 통과했는데 실제로는 결함이 남아 있던 경험에서 출발해, AI의 자기 보고를 기계가 반증하게 만든 세 가지 방법(돌연변이 테스팅, 훅, 에이전트 팀)을 공유합니다. ​ 발표 대상 AI가 만든 코드와 테스트를 검증하는 방법에 관심 있는 분 여러 AI 에이전트를 활용한 개발·리뷰에 관심 있는 분 ​ 목차 AI가 만든 결과를 어떻게 확인하는가 구현이 아니라 검증이 병목이 된 이유 확인이 막히는 세 곳 1층 테스트의 문제: AI가 짠 테스트를 믿을 수 있는가 통과에는 두 가지가 있다 AI가 받은 목표와 우리가 원한 목표 한 줄을 지워 보는 방법과 그 결과 2층 규칙 준수의 문제: 규칙을 적으면 AI가 지키는가 문서에 적어 두었는데 그 순간에 건너뛴다 문서는 부탁이고 훅은 강제다 3층 자기검증의 문제: AI가 AI를 검증할 수 있는가 저자와 검증자를 겸하면 채점이 안 된다 에이전트 팀으로 분리를 구조에 남긴다 검사가 지나가지 않는 줄은 검사되지 않는다 팀이 스스로 역할 정의를 고쳐 간다 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: OmniEvaluator: AI 모델과 에이전트를 위한 통합 평가 프레임워크
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 발표 내용 AI 서비스를 만들 때 "이 모델, 우리 서비스에 써도 될까?"라는 질문은 도입 전(후보 모델·API·툴 조합 비교)과 도입 후(의도대로 서빙되는지, 패치·버전별 차이) 반복해서 돌아옵니다. 그런데 이 질문에 답하는 비용은 큽니다. 모달리티마다 평가 툴킷이 다르고, 같은 벤치마크라도 프롬프트·파서·메트릭 구현에 따라 점수가 수십 점씩 갈라지며, 결과는 사람 손으로 모아야 합니다. ​ OmniEvaluator는 이 문제를 구조적으로 푸는 통합 평가 프레임워크입니다. 추론 엔진 4종(HF Transformers·vLLM·SGLang·상용 API)과 평가 프레임워크 4종(lm-eval-harness·lmms-eval·VLMEvalKit·built-in)을 하나의 중간 스키마로 연결해 텍스트·이미지·비디오·오디오 1,000개 이상의 벤치마크를 하나의 인터페이스로 실행합니다. 모든 실행은 설정·예측·점수를 담은 아티팩트로 남아 그대로 재현할 수 있고, CPU에서 도는 내장 Verifier가 프롬프트·프레임워크 차이에 흔들리지 않는 채점 신호를 제공합니다. 2026년에는 Agent Harness가 추가되어 기존 벤치마크에 옵션 두 개만 붙이면 툴 호출 궤적까지 채점하는 Agent 평가로 전환되며, 대시보드에서 요청 → 진행 → 결과 → 샘플을 한곳에서 확인할 수 있습니다. ​ 관련 자료 논문: A Composable Evaluation System for Reproducible Omni-Modal Foundation Model Evaluation (EMNLP 2026 System Demonstrations, arXiv 2609.01315) 공개 저장소 : https://github.com/naver-ai/omni-evaluator ​ 발표 대상 AI 서비스 기획자: 서비스 도입 전 후보 모델·API·툴 조합의 구현 가능성과 가치를 정량적으로 비교하려는 분 AI Engineer / Forward Deployment Engineer: 도입 후 모델이 의도대로 서빙되는지, 패치·버전·서빙엔진별 차이를 정량 확인하려는 분 모델 평가 담당자: 여러 모달리티·프레임워크에 걸친 평가 환경을 하나로 통합하려는 분 ​ 목차 평가의 어려움 OmniEvaluator 구조 Agent Harness 대시보드 — 리더보드, 샘플 뷰어, Trigger Claude Plugin 팀 운영 사례 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: AI 신입사원을 뉴스 데이터 시니어로 키우는 레포, news-data
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 AI 에이전트가 뉴스 데이터를 직접 찾고 추출·분석까지 수행하는 하네스 레포 news-data를 소개합니다. 작업마다 배운 것을 회고와 PR로 되돌려 도메인을 모르는 신입사원 같은 에이전트를 시니어로 키우는 과정과 운영하며 부딪힌 한계, 앞으로의 방향을 공유합니다. ​ 발표 대상 코딩 에이전트에게 사내 도메인 업무를 맡겨 보고 싶은 개발자 흩어진 데이터 문서와 도메인 지식을 정리하고 싶은 데이터 엔지니어·분석가 AGENTS.md, 스킬, 규칙으로 에이전트의 작업 방식을 설계해 보고 싶은 분 ​ 목차 1. 왜 만들었나 스키마만으로는 알 수 없는 컬럼의 의미, wiki·GitHub·코드 주석에 흩어진 문서, 담당자 머릿속의 노하우. SQL과 Spark는 잘 쓰지만 우리 조직의 사정은 모르는, 똑똑한 AI 신입사원의 문제 ​ 2. 어떻게 키우나 처음부터 다 모으지 않고 실제 업무를 맡기며, 작업마다 회고를 쓰고 PR로 레포에 되돌리는 작업 루프. 규칙 로드 · 스킬 선택 · 요청·데이터 파악 · 승인 후 실행·검증 · 회고·반영, 요청 한 건이 처리되는 다섯 단계. 그 결과 업무 40건 처리, 이슈부터 회고 PR까지 중앙값 1.6시간, 데이터 분석가 수준의 심층 분석까지 ​ 3. 어디까지 왔나 검토 병목 · 정합성 · 방향성, 키우면서 부딪힌 세 가지 한계. 그리고 계획과 실행을 리모트 데이터 에이전트로 옮기는 다음 단계 ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: 새벽 3시 54분, Agent가 먼저 분석하고 처리했습니다
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 발표 내용 개발과 운영 당번을 함께 맡으며 새벽 알림에 깨는 일, 언제까지 사람이 해야 할까요? 원인을 찾는 일부터 직접 조치하는 일까지 AI Agent에게 안심하고 맡길 수 있도록 풀어 간 경험을 공유 드립니다. ​ 발표 대상 개발과 서비스 운영(온콜)을 함께 맡고 있는 개발자·엔지니어 AI Agent에게 조사·조치 같은 실제 운영 업무를 맡기려는 개발자 사내 Agent 도입을 검토하는 팀 ​ 목차 도입 - 어느 조직에나 있는 문제 운영 대상은 늘고, 사람은 준다 온콜이 실제로 하는 일 열한 달의 여정 조사하는 Agent - 1단계 맡기려 했지만, 줄 게 없었다 ① 알림을 한 곳으로 ② 기억과 지식을 준다 응답 형식 케이스 ① 조사하는 Agent 손을 쓰는 Agent - 2단계 넘어야 할 질문 셋 Q1 뭘 할 수 있나 - 능력 Q2 언제 해도 되나 - 판정 Q3 틀리면 어떻게 되나 - 안전망 케이스 ② 무인 조치와 3장 정리 결론 어떻게 도는가 Agent의 진화와 운영 결과 앞으로 Takeaway ​ ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: 뇌를 닮은 세컨드 브레인: 토큰 낭비 없는 RAG
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 발표 내용 기존 RAG의 텍스트 덤프 및 토큰 낭비 한계를 극복하고, 최신 인지 메모리 논문 기법을 결합해 지식 자율 진화와 99% 재현율을 달성하는 차세대 AI 메모리 아키텍처를 소개합니다. ​ 발표 대상 RAG의 검색 효율과 답변 품질 개선에 관심 있는 개발자 AI 에이전트의 메모리 관리와 토큰 비용 절감에 관심 있는 개발자 ​ 목차 요청마다 다시 읽히는 토큰 다시 읽는 토큰 가운데 실제로 쓰이는 비율 넣은 4k 토큰 가운데 정답 근거의 비율 목차에서 잘린 규칙을 모델이 열어 보지 않는 문제 쓰지도 않는 토큰이 비싼 이유 크기 × 요청 수로 불어나는 비용 식 늘 넣기, 위치만 두기, 빼 두기: 무엇을 늘 넣어 둘까 Haema(해마)의 구조 층 구조: 기억 저장, 불러오기, 작업 기억, 세션 나누기, 판정 게이트 질문 하나가 지나는 여섯 단계 긴 대화를 위한 세션 롤오버와 기존 compact의 차이 기본값을 바꾸는 판정 게이트 만들고 나서 측정한 결과 대표 실측 넷: 문장 고르기, 중복 제거, 통째로 넣는 RAG와의 비교, 세션 롤오버 통째로 넣는 RAG와 Haema의 재현율·토큰 비교 긴 코딩 과제에서 본 토큰과 기억 시험 다른 장치들: 두 단 목차, 후속 질문 풀어 쓰기, 합치지 않고 쌓기 우리 팀에 적용하기 실험에서 뽑은 여덟 가지 지금 버전이 나오기까지 거친 세 번의 판정 지금 기본으로 쓰는 것과 선택 설정 먼저 측정해 볼 세 가지 비율과 장치를 붙일 수 있는 자리 우리 팀의 RAG와 에이전트에 던져 볼 질문 네 가지 다시 읽히는 토큰에게 '쓰이고 있니?'를 묻기 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.
