title: Jetpack Compose 기반 커스텀 3D 캐러셀 개발기 (영상)
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 가로로 넘기는 목록을 만들 때 대부분 LazyRow부터 떠올립니다. 하지만 카드가 비스듬히 겹겹이 쌓이고, 넘길 때마다 간격과 기울기가 바뀌는 3D 카드 덱은 LazyRow로 만들 수 없었습니다. 이 발표에서는 ThingsBook 서비스 내의 카드 덱 UI를 LazyRow 없이 Jetpack Compose로 직접 만들면서 겪은 세 가지 이슈와 해결 과정을 공유합니다. ​ 매 프레임 바뀌는 값을 리컴포지션 없이 화면에 반영하는 방법 3D로 기울인 UI의 터치 영역이 어긋나는 버그를 추적하고, 직접 판정으로 해결한 과정 LazyRow 없이 Paging3의 다음 페이지 로드를 제어한 방법 ​ 발표 대상 Jetpack Compose 기반 복잡한 인터렉션을 포함한 UI 개발에 관심 있는 Android 개발자 Jetpack Compose 관련 성능, 설계, 이슈에 대해 관심 있는 Android 개발자 복잡한 UI 를 AI 를 활용해 만들고 싶은 개발자 ​ 목차 ​ 문제의 UI: LazyRow로 만들 수 없었던 카드 덱 왜 LazyRow가 아닌가: 배치·스크롤·보이는 것만 컴포즈, 세 가지 약속 카드 덱의 동작 원리: Float 하나로 모든 카드를 움직이는 구조 이슈 ① 리컴포지션 0으로 매 프레임 움직이기 이슈 ② 3D로 기울인 UI의 터치 판정 이슈 ③ LazyRow 없이 Paging3 다루기 AI와 함께 만들기: 빨라진 것, 그리고 안 됐던 것 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: 디자인 시스템이 있는데도 화면은 왜 제각각일까?
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스뱅크에서 대출 심사 플랫폼을 디자인하는 Product Designer 신재희입니다. 대출 심사 플랫폼은 대출 신청 건을 검토하고 처리하는 내부 업무 툴이에요. 이 툴은 대출 상품마다 화면이 제각각이었고, 저는 이걸 하나의 구조로 묶는 일을 맡게 되었는데요. 오늘은 복잡한 업무 툴에 일관성을 만들기 위해 무엇을 이해하고, 어떻게 기준을 세웠는지를 이야기해 보려고 해요. 같은 업무인데, 화면은 제각각인 툴 대출 심사 플랫폼은 대출 운영 담당자가 매일 사용하는 업무 툴이에요. 담당자들은 이곳에서 대출 신청 건을 열어 정보와 서류에 문제가 없는지, 다음 단계로 넘어가도 되는지를 확인하죠. 팀에 처음 합류해 제품을 써 봤을 때 가장 먼저 느낀 건 일관성이 없다는 거였어요. 신용대출, 주택담보대출 등 대출 상품별로 처리 흐름이 다른 건 자연스러운 일이지만, 같은 목적의 행동까지 상품마다 다른 방식으로 만들어져 있었다는 게 문제 였어요. 예를 들어 대출 심사는 크게 신청자 정보 확인, 서류 검토, 각 단계의 결과 확정 순서 로 진행돼요. 이때 확정 은 심사 과정에서 중요한 행동이에요. 그런데 이 버튼이 주택담보대출에서는 화면 하단의 가장 우측, 전세자금대출에서는 좌측 안에 놓여 있었어요 . 단계마다 주요 과업 버튼이 노출되는 방식도 상품별로 제각각이었고요. 운영 담당자가 주택담보대출을 담당하다가 전세대출팀으로 옮기면, 같은 업무를 하더라도 버튼의 위치와 사용 방식부터 다시 익혀야 했죠. 새로운 화면에 적응하고 교육하는 데 시간과 비용이 들었고, 그 부담은 고스란히 팀에 돌아갔어요. 디자인 시스템이 없던 것도 아니었어요. 버튼, 테이블, 필드 같은 기초 컴포넌트는 이미 있었죠. 그런데도 왜 이런 문제가 생겼을까요? 원인을 찾으려면 먼저 이 제품이 실제로 어떻게 쓰이고 있는지부터 이해해야 했어요. 고치기 전에, 먼저 이해하기 대출은 업무의 히스토리가 길고, 실수 하나가 큰 영향을 미치는 도메인이에요. 팀에 합류한 뒤 제품과 업무를 정확히 이해하기 위해 두 가지 방향으로 접근했어요. 1. 제품의 구조 분해하기 먼저 제품에서 수행해야 할 작업을 체크리스트로 만들었어요. 실제 개발 환경에서 체크리스트를 따라 과업을 하나씩 수행하며 제품을 파악해 보려 했죠. 그런데 같은 작업도 상품마다 화면 구성과 처리 방식이 달랐어요. 정해진 순서대로 체크리스트를 따라가는 것만으로는 각 상품의 흐름을 파악하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 서로 다른 대출 상품의 화면을 단계별로 캡처해 하나의 아트보드에 나란히 놓았어요. 세로에는 상품을, 가로에는 단계를 배치해 같은 단계끼리 비교했어요. 그러자 상품마다 다른 부분이 한눈에 보였어요. 예를 들어 같은 확인 단계인데도 어떤 상품은 모달로, 어떤 상품은 화면 안에서 바로 처리하고 있었어요. 이 차이를 PO와 엔지니어분들께 하나씩 여쭤봤어요. 업무상 필요해서 생긴 차이도 있었지만, 단순히 제품이 만들어진 시점이 달라서 생긴 차이도 있었어요. 이렇게 차이의 이유를 구분해 정리한 표가 이후 공통 패턴을 파악하는 출발점이 됐어요. 2. 사용자에게 직접 묻기 제품을 직접 써 보는 것만으로는 실제 업무 방식까지 파악하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 UX Researcher분의 도움을 받아 실제 운영 담당자분들을 인터뷰하며 일하는 모습을 가까이서 지켜봤어요. 그런데 제가 생각했던 업무 흐름과 실제로 일하는 방식이 크게 다르더라고요. 심사에는 단계가 있으니 업무도 순서대로 진행될 거라고 생각했어요. 정보를 확인하고, 다음 단계로 넘어가 서류를 보고, 마지막에 확정하는 식으로요. 그런데 실제 담당자분들은 앞 단계로 돌아가 다시 확인하기도 하고, 모니터 양쪽에 여러 화면을 띄워 둔 채 정보를 교차 검증하며 일하고 있었어요. 단계는 나뉘어 있었지만, 실제 업무가 그 순서대로만 진행되는 건 아니었죠. 이런 업무 방식을 관찰하면서 설계 방향도 달라졌어요. 순서대로 진행하는 흐름은 기본 패턴으로 두되, 교차 검증이 필요한 화면은 단계와 상관없이 언제든 조회할 수 있어야 했어요. 그래서 특정 화면을 새 창으로 띄우는 버튼처럼, 필요한 정보에 바로 접근할 수 있는 장치가 필요하다는 생각도 할 수 있었죠. 제품을 직접 써 보는 것만으로는 발견하기 어려웠던 요구사항이었죠. 인터뷰를 통해 알게 된 내용 팁: 인터뷰는 도메인을 익힌 다음에 고맥락 제품이라면 너무 이른 시점의 인터뷰는 추천하지 않아요. 쓰는 용어도, 일하는 방식도 일상에서 접하는 도메인과 많이 다르거든요. 인터뷰어가 도메인을 얼마나 이해하고 있느냐에 따라 들을 수 있는 이야기의 깊이가 달라져요. 컴포넌트는 있었지만 기준은 없었다 제품을 이해하고 나니, 무엇을 통일하고 무엇을 상품별로 다르게 가져가야 할지가 보였어요. 모든 상품의 화면을 똑같이 만드는 게 아니라, 여러 상품에서 반복되는 화면과 행동에 일관된 기준을 세우는 게 중요했죠. 그동안 이 툴은 전담 디자이너 없이 각 팀의 요청에 맞춰 빠르게 확장되어 왔어요. 기존 디자인 시스템의 컴포넌트를 활용하되, 화면을 어떻게 구성하고 배치할지는 각 팀이 상황에 맞게 판단해야 했죠. 빠른 대응이 우선이다 보니 공통된 기준을 세우기보다는 각자 필요한 방식으로 조합해 사용하는 일이 많았어요. 디자인 시스템은 있었지만, 이를 화면 단위로 어떻게 조합하고 배치할지에 대한 기준은 없었던 거예요. 그래서 컴포넌트를 더 만드는 대신, 여러 상품에서 반복되는 화면과 흐름을 화면 단위의 패턴으로 정의하기로 했어요. 대출 심사 과정에서 공통적으로 필요한 화면을 살펴보고, 크게 세 가지 패턴으로 나눴어요. 리스트 화면: 심사할 신청 건을 찾고 선택하는 화면 단계별 작업 화면: 신청자 정보와 서류를 검토하는 화면 부가 정보 영역: 교차 검증에 필요한 정보를 언제든 확인할 수 있는 영역 정의한 패턴은 제품 안에서 패키지화해 어떤 상품을 작업하든 가져다 쓸 수 있도록 만들었어요. 확정 같은 핵심 행동의 위치와 동작 방식도 패턴에 포함했어요. 기존 컴포넌트만으로 표현하기 어려운 부분은 새로운 구조를 만들어 보완했고요. 이렇게 화면 단위의 패턴까지 갖추면서 디자인 시스템을 확장할 수 있었어요. 덕분에 새 상품을 작업할 때마다 화면 구조를 처음부터 고민할 필요가 없어졌어요. 이미 정의된 패턴을 바탕으로 상품에 필요한 구성을 선택하고 조합하는 것부터 설계를 시작할 수 있게 됐죠. AI로 구축한 DLOS Docs 이렇게 합의한 패턴과 규칙은 문서로도 정리했어요. 이전에는 설계 결정이 업무 메신저와 여러 문서에 흩어져 있었어요. 누군가 물어볼 때마다 같은 설명을 반복해야 했고, 새 팀원이 오면 맥락을 처음부터 다시 공유해야 했죠. 그래서 AI를 활용해 패턴과 규칙을 한곳에서 확인할 수 있는 공통 문서를 만들었어요. 이제 규칙에 대한 질문이 생기면 문서를 바탕으로 대화를 시작할 수 있게 됐어요. 만드는 것보다 어려웠던 것, 설득 좋은 패턴을 만들었다고 바로 쓰이진 않더라고요. 당시 상품들은 비즈니스적으로 빠르게 성장하고 있었고, 디자인 시스템을 적용하는 일은 당장의 우선순위가 아니었어요. 이미 각자의 방식으로 운영되던 팀들을 설득하는 과정은 생각보다 길고 어려웠어요. 공통 패턴을 사용해야 한다고 여러 번 공유해도, 어느새 다른 곳에서 새로운 패턴이 만들어져 있었어요. 그럴 때마다 해당 사례를 다시 팀으로 가져와 함께 살펴보고 기준을 맞춰야 했죠. 처음에는 공통 구조를 적용해야 한다는 점을 말로써 강조만 했어요. 하지만 몇 차례 커뮤니케이션을 거치면서 PO, PM분들이 실제로 걱정하는 게 무엇인지 알게 됐어요. 바로 속도였어요. 공통 구조를 적용하려면 기존 방식을 바꾸고 새로운 구조를 익혀야 하니, 당장의 출시가 늦어질 수 있다는 거였죠. 그때부터는 각 팀이 걱정하는 부분에 공감하면서 장기적으로 드는 비용까지 함께 생각해 보자고 이야기했어요. 각자 만들면 당장의 출시는 빠를 수 있지만, 상품이 늘어날 때마다 같은 구조를 다시 만들어야 하고 운영 담당자가 바뀔 때마다 새로운 화면을 익혀야 하니까요. 반대로 공통 구조가 쌓이면 다음 상품은 이미 정해진 패턴을 활용해 더 적은 시간과 노력으로 만들 수 있어요. 이런 이야기를 나누면서 공통 구조가 플랫폼팀만을 위한 기준이 아니라, 각 상품팀의

title: Why Can’t My Running Pods Be Reached? Our Journey to kube-proxy nftables Mode
abstract: Hi, I’m Karin, and I’m on the Cluster squad within SRE at Karrot. Our team designs and runs the Kubernetes platform that every service at Karrot runs on. We take responsibility for everything that keeps our clusters observable and reliable, from monitoring infrastructure all the way to the service mesh and security, along with the policies and roadmaps that keep it all maintainable. In this post, I’ll share how we migrated kube-proxy from iptables mode to nftables mode. kube-proxy runs on every node in a Kubernetes cluster and programs network rules into the Linux kernel so that traffic sent to a Service reaches the actual Pods. For years, our clusters ran kube-proxy in iptables mode to provide this core feature. Below, I’ll walk through how we moved to nftables, its more efficient successor, and what we learned along the way. 1. kube-proxy latency was hurting service reliability In Kubernetes, nodes come and go and Pods spin up all the time. That’s just how it works. But when a Pod lands on a fresh node and the app starts up, is it actually ready to talk to other services? kube-proxy manages the network rules (just “rules” from here on) on each node that let traffic headed for a Service reach the actual Pods . On a new node, if an application starts up while those rules are still being prepared, its DNS lookups and calls to other services can fail. kube-proxy rule sync lag had been creeping up for a while. We’d been watching the metrics since 2024, and latency was noticeably higher in our production cluster in the Korea region, the largest of all the regions we serve. But we judged it wasn’t serious enough to cause operational problems, and in practice, it never actually turned into an incident. Then, in the first half of this year, we made a big change: we adopted Karpenter. Now that we could scale out nodes quickly, we stopped using the Overprovisioner that used to keep spare nodes ready for Pods. As a result, Pods were landing on freshly created nodes much more often, which also raised the odds that an application would try to talk to something before rule sync had finished. Soon after, we started getting reports like the ones below, and most of them boiled down to “my Pod can’t talk to anything.” Putting our kube-proxy metrics from 2024 and 2026 side by side made it obvious how much heavier kube-proxy’s workload had gotten in just two years. Our service footprint and NAT rule count had grown noticeably, and Pods were being created and terminated far more often. Every time a Pod changes, the Service’s Endpoints (the IPs of the Pods that receive its traffic) change with it, so the number of changes kube-proxy had to apply grew right along with it. Rule sync latency got several times worse, and endpoint changes pending, which tracks Endpoint changes not yet reflected in the rules, went from occasional brief spikes to a steady backlog. Latency and endpoint changes pending in 2024 Latency and endpoint changes pending in 2026 network programming rate in 2024 network programming rate in 2026 In the first half of 2026, our service cluster had roughly 1,400 Services and 27,000 Pods, with about 80,000 iptables NAT rules. With Endpoints constantly churning from deploys and autoscaling, and nodes repeatedly being torn down and spun up, the initial rule sync on a new node sometimes took as long as 4 minutes and 20 seconds . (That’s over four minutes with no working Service or DNS traffic!) Once we confirmed this was actually affecting production, we had to fix it. After some intense discussion with the team, we decided to try switching kube-proxy from iptables mode to nftables mode. Here’s how the two modes differ. In iptables mode, kube-proxy creates rules for every Service and every Endpoint. When a packet comes in, it’s first matched against the Service rules one by one, top to bottom, to find the destination Service, and then against that Service’s Endpoint rules, again one by one, to pick a Pod. title: 파드는 떴는데 왜 통신이 안 될까? kube-proxy nftables 전환 여정
abstract: 안녕하세요, 당근 SRE팀 클러스터 파트에서 일하고 있는 Karin(카린)이에요. 클러스터 파트는 당근 내부의 모든 서비스가 운영되는 쿠버네티스 환경을 설계하고 관리해요. 쿠버네티스 환경의 가시성과 서비스 안정성을 확보하기 위해 모니터링 인프라부터 서비스 메시, 보안까지 여러 방면에서 정책과 로드맵을 설계하고 적용해요. 이 글에서는 kube-proxy를 iptables 모드에서 nftables 모드로 전환한 이야기를 해보려고 해요. kube-proxy는 쿠버네티스의 모든 노드에서 동작하면서, Service로 들어온 트래픽이 실제 Pod로 전달되도록 리눅스 커널에 네트워크 규칙을 설정하는 컴포넌트예요. 이 규칙을 관리하는 방식으로 오랫동안 iptables를 써왔는데, 이를 더 효율적인 후속 도구인 nftables로 바꾼 과정과 그 과정에서 배운 점을 공유하려고 해요. 1. kube-proxy latency가 서비스 안정성에 영향을 미쳤어요 쿠버네티스에서 노드가 새로 생기고 Pod가 뜨는 것은 매우 자연스러운 일이죠. 그런데 새 노드에 Pod가 스케줄링되고 애플리케이션이 시작되었다고 해서, 다른 서비스와 통신할 준비도 모두 끝난 걸까요? kube-proxy는 각 노드에서 Service로 향하는 트래픽이 실제 Pod에 도달할 수 있게 네트워크 규칙(이하 ‘규칙’)을 관리 하는데요, 새 노드에서는 이 규칙을 준비하는 동안 애플리케이션이 먼저 시작하면 DNS 조회나 다른 서비스와의 통신에 실패할 수 있어요. kube-proxy의 규칙 동기화가 느려지고 있다는 것은 예전부터 알고 있었어요. 2024년부터 지표를 지켜보니, 다른 리전보다 규모가 큰 한국 프로덕션에서 유독 지연이 높았거든요. 그러나 운영상 문제가 될 정도는 아니라고 판단했고, 실제로도 이슈로 이어진 적은 없었어요. 하지만 올해 상반기에 Karpenter를 도입하는 큰 변화가 있었어요. 노드를 빠르게 scale-out할 수 있게 되면서 Pod가 사용할 노드를 미리 준비하던 Overprovisioner를 더 이상 사용하지 않게 됐어요. 그 결과 새로 생성된 노드에 Pod가 곧바로 스케줄링되는 상황을 더 자주 마주했어요. 규칙 동기화가 끝나기 전에 애플리케이션이 통신을 시도할 가능성도 커진 거죠. 이후에 아래와 같은 문의가 들어오기 시작했고, 대부분은 ‘Pod가 통신이 안 된다’라는 제보였어요. 2024년과 2026년의 kube-proxy 지표를 나란히 놓고 보니, 2년 사이 kube-proxy의 부담이 크게 늘어난 걸 뚜렷하게 확인할 수 있었어요. 서비스 규모와 NAT 규칙 수가 눈에 띄게 늘었고, Pod가 생성되고 종료되는 일도 잦아졌어요. Pod가 바뀔 때마다 Service의 목적지를 나타내는 Endpoint, 즉 트래픽을 받을 Pod의 IP도 함께 바뀌기 때문에 kube-proxy가 반영해야 할 변경도 그만큼 늘어났어요. 그 결과 규칙 동기화 지연은 이전보다 몇 배 커졌고, 아직 규칙에 반영되지 못한 Endpoint 변경을 나타내는 endpoint changes pending 지표도 과거에는 잠깐씩 튀던 값이 지속적으로 쌓이는 모습으로 바뀌었어요. 2024년의 latency와 endpoint changes pending 2026년의 latency와 endpoint changes pending 2024년의 network programming rate 2026년의 network programming rate 2026년 상반기 당시 서비스 클러스터에는 약 1,400개의 Service와 27,000개의 Pod가 있었고, iptables의 NAT 규칙은 약 80,000개에 달했어요. 배포와 오토스케일링으로 Endpoint가 계속 바뀌는 가운데, 노드가 반복적으로 종료되고 생성될 때는 첫 규칙 동기화에 최대 4분 20초 가 걸리기도 했어요. 4분 넘게 Service와 DNS 통신이 안 되는 상태였던 거예요! 실제 서비스 운영에 영향을 주는 문제라는 것을 확인했기 때문에 이 문제를 해결해야 했어요. 팀원들과 개선 방안을 치열하게 의논한 결과 iptables 모드에서 nftables 모드로 전환해 보기로 했어요. 두 모드의 차이점은 다음과 같아요. iptables 모드에서 kube-proxy는 Service마다, 그리고 Endpoint마다 규칙을 만들어요. 패킷이 들어오면 먼저 Service 규칙을 위에서부터 차례로 비교해 목적지 Service를 찾고, 다시 그 Service의 Endpoint 규칙을 차례로 비교해 보낼 Pod를 골라요. 두 단계 모두 순차 비교라서 Service가 많을수록, 그리고 Service 하나에 붙은 Endpoint가 많을수록 비교할 규칙이 늘어나 조회 비용이 O(N)이에요. 더 큰 문제는 규칙을 갱신할 때예요. 전체 규칙 수는 Service와 Endpoint 수에 비례하고, 규칙이 많을수록 갱신 시간도 길어져요. 그런데 Endpoint는 Pod가 변경될 때 함께 바뀌어서 갱신이 자주 일어나다 보니, 반영하지 못한 변경이 점점 쌓였어요. 특히 kube-proxy가 시작한 직후에는 전체 규칙을 새로 쓰는 full sync를 하는데, 규모가 커진 당근 클러스터에서는 이 시간이 4분을 넘기도 했어요. nftables 모드는 Service를 찾는 단계와 Endpoint를 고르는 단계를 모두 map 기반으로 처리해요. 목적지 IP . 프로토콜 . 포트를 키로 map을 조회해서 해당 Service로 바로 이동하고, Endpoint도 목록을 하나씩 훑지 않고 map에서 바로 골라요. 그래서 Service나 Endpoint가 늘어나도 조회 비용은 O(1)에 가깝게 유지돼요. 갱신할 때도 지난 동기화 이후 바뀐 Service와 Endpoint만 반영하므로, 비용이 전체 규모가 아니라 변경량에 비례해요. Endpoint가 많고 자주 바뀌는 환경일수록 이 차이가 크게 드러나요. 하지만 모드를 변경하기 전에, 몇 가지 질문이 있었어요. 무엇이 규칙 동기화를 느리게 만들고 있었을까요? Service와 Endpoint가 많아서일까요? 변경이 자주 발생해서일까요? nftables로 바꾸면 얼마나 개선될까요? nftables 모드로 ‘안전하게’ 전환할 수 있을까요? 이 질문에 답하기 위해, 테스트 클러스터에서 조건을 바꿔가며 latency를 측정하고 iptables와 nftables를 비교하는 실험을 해보기로 했어요. 첫 동기화 시간을 20초 이내로 줄여야 한다고 판단했고, 실험으로 이를 검증하고자 했어요. 2. 실험의 네 가지 목표 실험을 시작하기 전에, 이 프로젝트에서 무엇을 확인할지 네 가지로 정리했어요. 1. 조건에 따른 규칙 동기화 지연 시간 확인 Service와 Endpoint가 많은 것과, 그 Endpoint가 자주 바뀌는 것은 다른 조건이겠죠? 같은 수의 Pod를 배포하더라도 조금씩 교체할 때와 한꺼번에 교체할 때의 영향이 다를 수 있고요. 규모, 변경 빈도, 배포 패턴을 나눠서 각각 latency에 어떤 영향을 주는지 측정해보기로 했어요. 2. 같은 조건에서 iptables와 nftables를 비교 nftables의 성능이 좋다고 알려져 있어도, 당근의 운영 환경에서 얼마나 개선될지는 직접 확인하고 싶었어요. 테스트 클러스터에서 같은 부하를 만들어 성능을 비교하기로 했어요. 3. 프로덕션에 안전하게 적용할 수 있는지 확인 테스트에서 빨라졌다고 바로 전환할 수는 없겠죠? 당근에서 사용하는 VPC CNI, Istio 등의 addon 구성과 충돌 없이 동작하는지, 알려진 이슈 중 우리 환경에 해당하는 것은 없는지 살펴봐야 했어요. 4. kube-proxy 버전을 유지할지, 함께 업그레이드할지 당시 EKS는 v1.34이지만, kube-proxy는 v1.34에서 이슈( https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135323 )가 발견되어 v1.31을 유지하고 있었어요. v1.31에서도 nftables 모드를 사용할 수 있었기 때문에, 모드만 변경하는 방법과 v1.34로 올리면서 변경하는 방법을 모두 검토했어요. 버전마다 성능과 알려진 이슈가 다를 수 있으니, 개선 폭과 운영 위험을 함께 비교해 결정하고자 했어요. 3. 먼저, 무엇을 측정

title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
abstract: Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.

title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
abstract: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.

title: Text-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models for Multimodal Forecasting
abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.

title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
abstract: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $π_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $μ_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.

title: Agent-as-a-Verifier: From Scores to Evidence for General Verification
abstract: Verification is increasingly critical across various inference and learning paradigms, such as test-time scaling, recursive intelligence and automated research, where feedback can improve efficiency and optimization. Common score-based verifiers, or discriminative reward models, predict a scalar reward for an output. While useful for filtering, rewarding, and ranking, such scores provide no explicit, auditable evidentiary basis for the judgment. In parallel, although existing generative process reward models offer text feedback, most designs do not fully exploit agentic capabilities, such as tool use and iterative reasoning, which are essential for fact-checking and fine-grained claim verification. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing Agent-as-a-Verifier, an agentic, certificate-producing verification system that places role-separated LLM agents inside a formal-methods-inspired claim-obligation-certificate protocol. Given a generation candidate, Agent-as-a-Verifier produces a certificate by extracting a verdict-blind dependency graph of claims, independently compiling the task's acceptance contract, and deriving checkable obligations. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, Agent-as-a-Verifier achieves higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art approach. Across different downstream applications, the augmented agent also outperforms the plain agent on FrontierMath and CyberGym. More importantly, Agent-as-a-Verifier is able to identify reward-hacking solutions that deceive the benchmark evaluator, highlighting its broader potential for iterative and recursive agent optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/sunyxedu/General-Verifier

title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
abstract: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

title: On the Learnability of Model Reprogramming: A Reachability and Relabeling Perspective
abstract: Model reprogramming adapts a frozen source model to a target task by wrapping it in a learnable input transformation from target input to the source-model input space, and an output mapping from source-model outputs to target predictions. Despite extensive empirical progress, the finite-sample learnability of the induced wrapper hypothesis class $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ remains underexplored. We address this for source models that expose hard source labels and analyze it through the wrapper structure: on any target samples, the input transformation selects reachable source labels that the output mapping relabels. Through this lens, we answer two questions: (1) how many target samples are needed to approach the best predictor in $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$, and (2) what gap remains between the optimum over $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ and the target Bayes risk. For (1), the wrapper structure factorizes the sample-wise complexity of $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ into a reachability term counting reachable source-label patterns, and a conditional relabeling term counting their relabelings. This yields an agnostic-PAC bound on the estimation error, with sample complexity scaling additively in the two terms; this bound becomes closed-form on additive input transformations and is matched by a lower bound on an explicit binary classification construction. For (2), the same structure decomposes the approximation error exactly into the source-label information loss and output-mapping restriction with a source-conditional upper bound on this gap. We extend the approximation analysis to logit-exposing source models, where the upper bound is empirically estimable. The wrapper-side analysis localizes both errors to specific components, giving a structural view of reprogramming practice.

title: Ensuring Deployment-Time Safety of Neural Network Controlled Systems via Localized Certificate Repair
abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.

title: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression
abstract: Many deep learning models exhibit a double-descent phenomenon, where test loss exhibits a sharp peak near the interpolation threshold and then descends a second time as model size grows further, contrary to the U-shape predicted by the classical bias--variance tradeoff. The double-descent phenomenon has been found and explained in toy classical models, but is not well-understood in modern deep learning despite extensive empirical study. We interpret double descent through the novel lens of universal compression. Specifically, we upper bound the maximum-likelihood excess test loss as a sum of four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and an MLE-vs-Bayes gap. Under exact posterior sampling, we further show that the expected MLE-vs-ensemble gap lower-bounds the MLE-vs-Bayes gap in the well-specified setting. In our experiments, a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation to the Bayes predictor, unlike SGD, shows no pronounced interpolation peak. Experiments with uniform random labels support this gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak; here, the SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy at the peak, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near $\log 10$.

title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
abstract: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.

title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability
abstract: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.

title: Online Identification Can Replace a Floor-Plan Prior on Unseen Buildings
abstract: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 °C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.

title: Pretraining for Forecasting in Relational Databases
abstract: Real-world forecasting increasingly relies on asynchronous transaction logs in relational databases rather than uniformly sampled arrays. While relational deep learning (RDL) models can forecast from these complex histories, they are typically trained separately for each specific target and root entity type. We introduce Query-Conditioned Relational pretraining (QCRP), a self-supervised framework that enables a standard RDL backbone to act as a universal forecaster across a database. QCRP generates diverse forecasting objectives using a structured temporal query grammar and interleaves them through a shared conditional predictor. This produces a robust, frozen encoder reusable for downstream tasks via lightweight predictors or a zero-shot interface. Evaluated on large-scale RelBench databases, QCRP learns frozen representations that support competitive forecasting across tasks and entity types. Furthermore, a single unified QCRP model checkpoint is competitive with isolated, entity-specific specialists. We demonstrate promising results for reusing the learned representations from standard RDL backbones for forecasting tasks in relational databases.

title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
abstract: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $ε$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-γ)^{-1},(1-γ)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $γ$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-γ)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $δ\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.

title: Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning for Backdoor Removal
abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a severe threat to modern NLP models by embedding hidden triggers that induce malicious behavior at inference time. Recent unlearning methods such as gradient ascent (GA) attempt to remove backdoors by maximizing the loss on poisoned samples; however, these methods can suffer from a critical limitation: they may shift the trigger's influence to other classes rather than eliminating it. In this work, we propose Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (TICU), a framework for mitigating textual backdoor behavior by enforcing prediction and representation invariance to trigger insertion. TICU constructs clean and trigger-inserted counterfactual pairs, then fine-tunes the model so that both inputs produce consistent output distributions and aligned hidden representations. To preserve clean-task performance, TICU also retains the supervised classification loss on clean data and constrains parameter drift from the original model. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets, model architectures, and attack settings show that TICU improves triggered accuracy and reduces trigger-induced prediction shifts compared with existing baselines, while maintaining competitive label-flipping performance and limiting clean-task degradation.

title: Casper: A Projection-Based Neurosymbolic Layer for Scalable & Guaranteed Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: Many real-world problems demand exact constraint satisfaction to be meaningfully solved, yet existing neurosymbolic methods face a stark trade-off: those that guarantee satisfaction fail to scale, while those that scale must resort to approximation. Meanwhile, traditional deep learning approaches offer no satisfaction guarantees at all. In this paper, we propose Casper, a neurosymbolic layer that simultaneously (i) guarantees constraint satisfaction, (ii) scales at inference time, (iii) is fully automated, requiring no problem-specific engineering, and (iv) is fully differentiable, making it composable with any neural predictor both at training and at inference time. Casper casts constraint satisfaction as a closed-form Euclidean projection onto the constraint-feasible region, computable in a single forward pass. Experiments across MNIST arithmetic (up to 1024 digits), Sudoku solving, and Warcraft pathfinding show that Casper is the only method that produces guaranteed-valid outputs at scale: on $30\times30$ Warcraft grids, exact baselines time out and approximate ones produce valid paths less than 7% of the time, while Casper produces them 100% of the time.

title: On the Impact of Extra Information in Bandit Learning: More is Not Always Merrier
abstract: More data is commonly assumed to improve learning performance, however, we show that this intuition can surprisngly fail in sequential decision-making. Considering a stochastic bandits setup with exogenous extra information, we ask if the free and unbiased extra reward samples are guaranteed to reduce the regret of the learner. We introduce a formal notion of `non-degradation under extra information' and demonstrate that the widely used Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB) violates this property, i.e., there exist benign extra-information under which UCB incurs strictly higher regret than when run without extra information. We contrast this behaviour with Thompson Sampling and Explore-Then-Commit, which appear to benefit from the same extra information. Constructively, we propose a meta-algorithm that provably enforces non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms. We also run empirical simulations to study our meta-algorithm.

title: Centered Kernel Distance: Dimension-Free Error Bounds for Comparing Neural Representations
abstract: The asymptotic error of representational similarity metrics such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) has been well-characterized, but there are no realistic bounds on how estimates of representational similarity $\textit{simultaneously}$ depend on the number of sampled neurons ($N$) and experimental conditions ($M$). We study the natural metric counterpart of CKA and RSA, which we call the Centered Kernel Distance (CKD). We show that CKD admits an unbiased estimator, whereas several popular similarity measures including CKA have no unbiased estimator. Under mild assumptions, we show that estimation error of CKD decays in proportion to $1/M + 1/N$. Strikingly, the rate in this bound does not depend on the dimensionality of the space of experimental conditions. Thus, similarity estimation does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, which plagues similar problems in high-dimensional statistics. We verify our results empirically in random shallow neural networks, trained neural networks, and macaque visual cortex data. Ultimately, this paper advances a framework for predicting the error of similarity estimators in experiments by relaxing existing, biologically-unrealistic assumptions. Our theoretical and empirical predictions produce specific prescriptions on how to most efficiently estimate the similarity between multiple neural systems.

title: Temporal Selective Exploration for Reinforcement Learning-Guided Continuous-Discrete Flow Matching in 3D Molecular Design
abstract: Flow matching has shown strong potential in generative tasks, while its optimization via Reinforcement Learning (RL) remains underexplored, especially in continuous-discrete mixed settings. Moreover, flow matching is formulated as an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE), whose deterministic trajectories do not naturally support RL optimization. Introducing stochasticity by converting the entire trajectory into a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) is a common practice. Nevertheless, not all timesteps contribute to the final outcomes, and redundant exploration introduces additional noise. Furthermore, in multi-objective settings, some objectives may dominate the optimization while others receive insufficient updates. In this study, we propose an RL-guided continuous-discrete flow matching framework with temporal selective exploration for 3D de novo molecular design. Specifically, our method jointly optimizes continuous and discrete flow matching for atomic coordinates and molecular identities, respectively, while restricting exploration to timesteps that primarily contribute to target properties, reducing ineffective exploration. We also introduce a reward-based advantage calibration mechanism to mitigate objective dominance in multi-objective optimization. The framework is applied to design inhibitors for both the well-studied target protein EGFR and the challenging Pin1 protein. We identify some novel candidate inhibitors, supported by in silico validation.

title: Best-of-$N$ Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging. Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of-$N$ test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment. We show that increasing $N$ does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking. We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a $π_{0.5}$ policy, with ten repetitions per case. We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as $N$ increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking. We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.

title: Benchmarking Segmentation Models for Scalable Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-1/2 Imagery
abstract: Mangroves are dynamic coastal ecosystems that contribute to carbon storage, coastal protection and biodiversity conservation, but are vulnerable to climate change. Very-high-resolution imagery such as Pléiades enables detailed mangrove mapping but it is costly and have a low revisit rate. Large-scale monitoring requires free and regularly available data such as Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 but their spatial resolution poses challenges for detailed mangrove mapping. In this work, we benchmark deep learning approaches for mangrove mapping from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery using reference maps derived from very-high-resolution Pléiades imagery. We compare four segmentation configurations based on CROMA and BigEarthNet-pretrained ResNet50 representations with different segmentation decoders. We construct a mangrove mapping dataset covering French Guiana, Suriname, and Amapá. CROMA + UPerNet achieves the best performance, with an F1-score of 0.9218 and an IoU of 0.8549. These results highlight the potential of pretrained multimodal Earth observation representations and open Sentinel data to support mangrove resilience through scalable monitoring.

title: The Marauder's Map: Bézier Manifolds Reveal Hidden Surfaces for Model Merging and Ensembling
abstract: Neural circuits are famously more robust than deep networks. This is often explained through degeneracy, where structurally distinct configurations support the same function. However, real biological systems exhibit a more flexible form of degeneracy in which specialized circuits continually adapt towards new competencies through localized changes while preserving existing function. Deep learning studies degeneracy through mode connectivity, which connects same-task networks by low-loss curves, sheets, or volumes. However, the field lacks a counterpart to flexible degeneracy, which demands more than ordinary mode connectivity. Defining such an analogue requires asking whether many independently initialized models trained on distinct tasks can be connected by a high-dimensional region of multi-task solutions. We introduce $\textit{Nimbus}$, which learns a high-dimensional Bézier manifold connecting $N$ specialists, going beyond the one-dimensional paths and two-dimensional sheets of mode connectivity work. A naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with $N$, but $\textit{Nimbus}$ requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders, showing that the connecting manifold has surprisingly low complexity yet supports multi-task competencies. The resulting manifold forms a navigable "Marauder's Map" that connects specialist models through a shared geometry of competent solutions. Trained across vision and language domains, $\textit{Nimbus}$ produces manifolds that are functionally and locally weight-flat: ensembles sampled from them degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in NLL loss and calibration error. $\textit{Nimbus}$ supplies a deep learning interpretation of flexible degeneracy, recasting model connectivity from a low-dimensional path between distant solutions into a high-dimensional volume of nearby ones.

title: When precision exceeds fidelity: systematic error quantification for inference with misspecified simulators
abstract: As scientific datasets grow in complexity and precision, the primary source of uncertainty in parameter inference shifts from measurement noise to systematic errors within the simulators themselves. In this setting, Bayesian evidence concentrates on whichever misspecified model best approximates the data. Evidence-weighted model averaging can then underestimate systematic uncertainty when one model component compensates for the misspecification of another component. We posit that in this case, the key question is how each model responds to discrepancies between simulator and data. We show that the local response of an inferred parameter to perturbations in the data --- the model's influence map --- can be estimated efficiently from forward evaluations of the simulator at existing posterior samples. Propagating discrepancy residuals through these influence maps enables individual sources of systematic bias to be isolated. Applied to independent observations used to infer the mass of a supermassive black hole, we find that the error is dominated by model systematics. We identify a simplification shared by all models, propagate the discrepancies through each model's influence map, and apply a first-order correction of the resulting biases. This substantially improves the cross-observation consistency of the inferred black-hole mass within each model while preserving the between-model spread that represents remaining systematics.

title: Auditing the Judge: Human-Derived Bias Discovery, Quantification, and Mitigation in LLM Judges
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators in evaluation and training pipelines, their judgements are often affected by systematic biases that conflict with human preferences. Although prior work has identified various biases and proposed methods for detecting and mitigating them, less attention has been paid to using human preferences to inform bias identification and mitigation. Moreover, these approaches rely heavily on pre-discovered bias lists, overlook bias strength, and depend on costly interventions. In this work, we propose HUB-J, an integrated framework based on human-derived bias factors that detects, quantifies, and mitigates biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Our approach leverages human-LLM judgement disagreement cases to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, and utilizes agreement cases to quantify bias strength through controlled input modifications and resulting shifts in model decisions. Finally, building on these quantified biases, we introduce a lightweight, training-free regression-based mitigation strategy that estimates the influence of each bias factor on model judgments and corrects bias-influenced decisions by removing its estimated effect. Empirical results show that HUB-J uncovers both known and novel bias factors, reveals meaningful differences in model susceptibility, and consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models.

title: Latent Merger: Latent-Space Composition of Hypernetwork-Generated LoRAs
abstract: Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.

title: Field Life: Particle Life as Interacting Chemical Fields
abstract: Field Life is a cellular automaton inspired by the interaction dynamics of Particle Life. In Particle Life, each particle has a colour, and an interaction matrix sets how strongly each colour attracts or repels each other colour. In Field Life, each colour is a channel of the automaton, and each cell holds a concentration of every colour. One step of the rule has three parts. Each colour is convolved with a ring-shaped kernel, which measures how much of that colour surrounds a cell. The interaction matrix combines these measurements into an attraction for each colour. The mass of each colour then moves toward higher attraction, in a way that conserves mass. A random matrix and a random initial state are usually enough to produce moving structure: bodies that glide, bodies that shed diffuse clouds, and gliders that break up into smaller gliders. We sample rules at random, keep the rules that move and form structure, and describe the patterns that appear: colours that sort into regions, colours that form stripes, and gliders, compact bodies that travel across the grid. The simulation and 120 saved rules, which we call worlds, are released.

title: E(n)-Equivariant Spherical Decision Surfaces
abstract: We present a constructive derivation of exactly E(n)-equivariant spherical decision surfaces by extending prior O(n)-equivariant hypersphere neurons to include translations. To achieve this, we present a decomposition of the features of the O(n)-equivariant neurons and provide explicit representations for translation and E(n)-transformations to fulfil the respective equivariance constraints. The resulting decision surfaces are exactly E(n)-equivariant without input centring or explicit pairwise differences, and admit explicit closed-form matrix representations. In addition, we numerically verify the correctness of the derivations and perform a downstream check of the resulting geometric primitives.

title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores
abstract: The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.

title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call $σ_{99}$), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.

title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.

title: ST-GNN-AAAS: Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for Anytime Automatic Algorithm Selection in the Traveling Salesman Problem
abstract: Anytime Automatic Algorithm Selection (AAAS) aims to make solver choices under varying time budgets. The existing AAAS approaches largely rely on static instance characteristics and make limited use of temporal information revealed during solver execution. We propose ST-GNN-AAAS, a Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network framework for AAAS in the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). The framework represents evolving incumbent tours using time-varying node features, including distances from each node to its neighbors in the current tour, and combines these features with solver performance observations over a short history window. Given this short history, ST-GNN-AAAS predicts solver selections over a longer future horizon. We evaluate the method on a subset of diverse TSP benchmarks from NATIONAL, TNM, TSPLIB, and VLSI, releasing the corresponding solver execution data to support reproducibility. Our model achieves a selection accuracy of 76.59% and closes 46.05% of the average rank gap between the single best solver (SBS) and the virtual best solver (VBS).

title: Contact Geometry for Generative Models: An Unbalanced Optimal Transport Formulation
abstract: Real-world generative problems in biology, medical imaging, or robotics, rarely come with perfectly paired source and target distributions. While unbalanced Optimal Transport (uOT) provides a robust framework to bridge unpaired datasets via minimum-length paths in probability space, existing formulations based on the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry introduce a structural bias toward high density regions, often triggering mode collapse. We introduce Contact unbalanced Optimal Transport (CuOT), a novel uOT formulation grounded in contact geometry that decouples density transport direction from mass growth to eliminate structural bias. This allows CuOT to adapt sampling steps to the local data structure, naturally reducing step sizes in high-density regions to prevent overshooting and ensuring stable convergence. The result is a stable, scalable path-length minimization solver that consistently outperforms WFR-based methods on biological dynamics reconstruction, unpaired image-to-image translation, and video generation.

title: A Description-Derived Drug-Drug Interaction Benchmark Reveals Split-Dependent Molecular Representation Rankings
abstract: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction is clinically important and poses a distinct challenge for molecular representation learning. Unlike single-molecule property prediction, DDI requires a predictor to compose two molecular representations into a relational outcome. DrugBank provides curator-authored DDI descriptions rather than ready-made categorical labels, so a categorical prediction target must first be derived from the text. We construct a dataset of DDI pairs by mapping processed descriptions to six text-derived categories and define a benchmark with four holdout regimes that restrict train-test chemical overlap from random pairs to scaffold-disjoint evaluation. We then use this benchmark to compare molecular fingerprints, pretrained sequence representations, and graph-derived features across five seeds and multiple classifier heads. Molecular fingerprints lead the high- overlap random split, whereas graph-derived representations lead the drug- and scaffold-holdout regimes, with the gap increasing as molecular overlap is restricted. Changing the classifier head affects absolute performance but not the relative representation ranking. These results show that representation rankings change with test-set novelty under a fixed description-derived label space.

title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.

title: ThinkMorph-SSL: Scaling Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning with Pretext Tasks
abstract: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.

title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination
abstract: Real-world applications of modern AI systems require generalization to both unseen environments and novel human users. The field of zero-shot coordination (ZSC) has focused primarily on deploying AI to cooperate with novel partners in otherwise familiar environments. Popular population-based methods achieve this by partnering the agent with a diversity of simulated human users during training in a fixed environment, but does not consider the more realistic scenario where both the users and the environment are unseen during training. Recently, training across environments has been explored in training a single self-play agent, which shows better generalization on both novel human users and unseen environments. In this work, we ask whether jointly modeling partner diversity and environment diversity yields stronger coordination with novel partners in novel environments. We introduce Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across a distribution of procedurally generated environments, and then trains a cooperator policy against this partner population. To further couple social and environmental reasoning, we add a next-state prediction module that encourages representations to encode both partner behavior and task structure. We evaluate CECP on both a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task, and the popular ZSC benchmark Overcooked, under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions. CECP achieves the strongest performance among the compared baselines and attains state-of-the-art results under our evaluation protocol for human-AI collaboration. We analyze the model's latent representation encoded by the next-state prediction module, showing it can not only improve the performance of the cooperative AI, but also provide more interpretable latents, demonstrated by the inference of partner skill levels.

title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.

title: Compressible Representations: Functional Spines in Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.

title: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset
abstract: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.

title: Tokenization and Architecture Jointly Allocate Component Roles in Time Series Transformers
abstract: Time series transformers have achieved strong forecasting performance, yet it remains unclear which of their components, attention or the feed-forward network (FFN), constructs temporal features, and how tokenization such as patching changes this. We propose a temporal probing framework that uses 15 token-level diagnostic tasks to measure feature construction as the gain in linear decodability of temporal properties from one sub-layer to the next (a matched MLP probe already saturates at the embedding). It targets models whose probed representations are read by a linear forecasting head. Applied to 5 supervised models trained on 8 long-term forecasting benchmarks, it finds that the constructing component is not fixed but allocated by the interaction of tokenization and architecture. Under patch tokenization (PatchTST), the FFN's gain exceeds attention's in probing on all 8 datasets, and its 8-dataset mean is 3.2x attention's. Without attention, the FFN alone reaches nearly the same total gain, both when attention is removed from a trained model and when PatchTST is trained without it, and the retrained model forecasts within a few percent of the full model. In probing, attention dominates under variate tokenization (iTransformer); in CATS, cross-attention is the only input path. In a controlled manipulation of PatchTST, single-scalar tokens (P=1) nearly eliminate the FFN's construction, while one more point per token (P=2) restores it. Our forecasting-side interventions (activation patching, knockout, and training without attention) establish component-level reliance and sufficiency. These results offer a representational reading of prior findings on the gains from patching, the competitiveness of self-attention-free models (TSMixer, PatchMLP), and the distinct role of cross-attention in CATS.

title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
abstract: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier

title: XRL4T1D: A Post-hoc Explainability Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Type 1 Diabetes Management
abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) requires lifelong insulin therapy, and reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for automated dosing in the UVA/Padova simulator. However, the decisions of RL controllers remain difficult to interpret. We present XRL4T1D, a post-hoc explainability framework for evaluating pretrained insulin-dosing policies without retraining. Each policy uses 60 minutes of continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and administered-insulin history, sampled every 5 minutes, to recommend insulin. We use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to compare the importance of CGM and insulin-history inputs and summarize insulin-history attributions over three 20-minute windows motivated by insulin-on-board. We assess whether these attributions correspond to policy-output sensitivity through targeted input replacement and compare temporal rankings with TimeSHAP. In all 80 patient-policy-mask-size cases, replacing the highest-attribution inputs changes the normalized insulin recommendation more than replacing the lowest-attribution or random inputs. The highest-attribution insulin-history window is also the most output-sensitive in 115 of 120 patient-policy-scenario configurations, and KernelSHAP and TimeSHAP select the same top window in 111 of 120. Applying XRL4T1D to PPO and G2P2C across 20 virtual patients, we find that both controllers rely predominantly on CGM history, especially G2P2C. However, the distribution of insulin-history importance across recent, middle, and older windows varies by cohort, explainer, and analysis settings, without a consistent separation between controllers. Global feature-attribution rankings remain stable under the tested observation corruptions. These results show why attribution fidelity, temporal reproducibility, and controller-comparison robustness should be assessed separately.

title: What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations
abstract: Recent advances in MLLMs have improved social understanding, enabling models to recognize emotions and distinguish truthful from deceptive behaviors. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on coarse-grained emotion recognition or binary truth-deception detection, overlooking the diverse ways people manipulate information in conversations, such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. Understanding these behaviors requires reasoning about underlying facts, participant knowledge, and conversational context, making them difficult to evaluate reliably. To address this gap, we introduce InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained information manipulation in conversations. InfoCon identifies six fine-grained strategies and derives a coarse consistency label from their factual and interactional relations. We develop an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework to construct and verify reliable labels from rich contextual evidence. We benchmark representative multimodal models and systematically analyze their fine-grained information manipulation understanding, providing a testbed beyond binary truth-deception judgments.

title: Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs
abstract: In recent years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved significant progress in chart-to-code generation. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on static charts, overlooking interactive charts that enable richer and more expressive data exploration. Unlike static chart-to-code generation, which emphasizes visual consistency, interactive chart-to-code evaluation targets behavioral consistency, requiring chart states to evolve correctly under sequences of user interactions, thereby rendering traditional one-step evaluation paradigms ineffective. To address this gap, we introduce ChartInt, the first benchmark specifically designed for interactive chart-to-code generation. ChartInt consists of 2,779 carefully annotated examples covering common interaction patterns such as hover, highlight, and tooltips. Additionally, ChartInt incorporates editing tasks such as data updates, style adjustments, and cross-chart style transfer to expand real-world application scenarios.
